top3.title: DEAD MEDIA (w/ filmmaker Joseph Scrimshaw in attendance)
top3.why: DEAD MEDIA is a horror-comedy about a haunted DVD and a movie night that refuses to end — a gnarly, affectionate homage to cult horror and the bygone era of DVD bonus features. Writer-director Joseph Scrimshaw is doing the screening in person, so you get the rare chance to grill the guy responsible for the haunted disc right after the credits roll. PhilaMOCA's cramped, velvet-dark former mausoleum showroom is exactly the room this movie was born to play in — doors around 7:00 PM, screening at 7:30.

top3.title: The Writing Room
top3.why: Three silent 40-minute writing sprints with 10-minute breaks and accountability check-ins between them — bring your own coffee and whatever project you've been avoiding, no genre or experience required. Iffy Books is South Philly's anarchist-adjacent DIY bookstore and reading room, so the space itself carries the same restless independent-press energy that makes it worth a visit even on a night with nothing scheduled. Free and low-key; you just have to actually write for two hours instead of talking about writing.

top3.title: Rustin's Challenge Reading Group
top3.why: A discussion of 'Rustin's Challenge,' which reconstructs Bayard Rustin's little-known economic vision — a jobs-centered 'Freedom Budget for All Americans' — as an alternative to what the organizers call the left's 'maximalist sloganeering.' Led by Paul Prescod at the Ethical Society's Rittenhouse Square home, it's the rare political reading group actually arguing tactics and history rather than trading vibes. Free, RSVP-based, and runs a tight two hours (6–8 PM) — easy to walk into cold even if you haven't read the book.

top3.title: NLG Know Your Rights Training
top3.cost: Free (typical for NLG trainings; not listed on page)
top3.why: The National Lawyers Guild runs a hands-on know-your-rights training at Philly's own anarchist radical bookstore, teaching what to do if police or ICE show up at your door, your job, or a protest. It's exactly the kind of practical, unglamorous organizing work that matters more this year than most, and Wooden Shoe has been a hub for exactly this since 1976 — no membership or affiliation required, just show up and learn. A rare case where a free evening at a bookstore might genuinely be useful to have sat through.

top3.title: Touki Bouki
top3.why: Djibril Diop Mambéty's 1973 Senegalese classic — a fever-dream about a cowherder and a student scheming to escape postcolonial Dakar for Paris — gets an honest-to-god theatrical screening as part of PFS's summer Road Trip series, rather than the usual grainy rip. It's routinely called one of African cinema's most audacious works, part political satire, part afro-punk fashion show. A 4:00 PM matinee is also available if evening doesn't work, but the 7:00 PM slot is the main event.

top3.title: Analog A/V Session
top3.why: Bring your dusty VHS tapes and cassette bootlegs — Iffy Books sets you loose with real analog-to-digital and digital-to-analog transfer gear, a scrappy hands-on session that fits nowhere else on the week's calendar. It's the exact overlap Iffy consistently delivers on: DIY electronics culture in a leftist-adjacent indie bookstore, run on a pay-what-you-can basis so nobody's priced out. Good excuse to finally digitize that box of mixtapes.

top3.title: The Body, with BIG|BRAVE, Carnivorous Bells
top3.why: The Body is one of the most punishing and inventive acts in experimental heavy music — two decades of Chip King and Lee Buford warping noise, doom, and black metal into something closer to horror-film sound design than a rock show — and Montreal's BIG|BRAVE bring their own cathedral-sized, slow-burning guitar drone to match. top3.why: A night of readings by disabled queer poets, in a scene that too often gets shut out of mainstream reading series entirely — this one's built specifically to center them. It's happening at Wooden Shoe Books, the volunteer-run anarchist collective bookstore that's been South Street's home for radical literature and community organizing since 1976, so the politics of the room match the politics of the work. Masks are required and the space is wheelchair accessible — access isn't an afterthought here, it's the point.

top3.title: The Magic City: Birmingham According to Sun Ra
top3.why: A documentary tracing Herman Poole Blount's path from segregated 1914 Birmingham to becoming Sun Ra, jazz's most gloriously strange cosmic philosopher — a portrait of both an artist and the city that shaped him before he left it behind. It screens at PhilaMOCA, a converted mausoleum turned microcinema that's the single best-matched venue in the city for exactly this flavor of outsider deep-cut. Doors at 7, film at 7:30, $12 at the door — a rare theatrical showing you won't find streaming anywhere.

top3.title: Iron Chic

top3.why: Iron Chic are Long Island melodic-punk lifers who've spent nearly two decades writing gut-punch anthems about dead-end towns and holding on anyway — real touring pedigree, playing a totally free, all-ages show right on the Delaware waterfront. No ticket, no cover, doors at 6 — that's about as rare as it gets for a band this well-traveled. Free punk on the harbor doesn't stay a secret long, so get there early.

top3.title: Inaugural North Philly Transit Rider Union Meeting
top3.venue: Joseph E. Coleman Northwest Regional Library
top3.why: This is the founding meeting of a brand-new North Philly transit riders' union, organizing residents around SEPTA service, fares, and accessibility — the kind of ground-floor labor organizing you don't get a second shot at once the group already exists. It's happening in a neighborhood library branch instead of a downtown conference room, which tells you exactly who this union is built for. Free, open to anyone who rides the bus or the El and wants a say in how it's run.

top3.title: Shadowplay x Synthicide pres. The 1st Annual Daytime Tropigoth Festival
top3.address: 211 S Christopher Columbus Blvd, Philadelphia, PA 19106
top3.why: Two Philly promoters known for keeping the goth and darkwave scene alive — Shadowplay and Synthicide — team up for a brand-new daytime crossover: Italo disco, synthpop, hi-NRG, new wave, and freestyle spun by five DJs on the waterfront. Being billed as the '1st Annual' means this is a genuine one-off this year, not a rerun of something you can catch next month. Runs 3-10pm at Liberty Point for a very reasonable $18.28 and up, dark-culture energy in broad daylight.

top3.title: Anarchy Summer Reading Group: 'The Utopia of Rules' by David Graeber (2nd half)
top3.why: Iffy Books' biweekly anarchist reading group works through the second half of David Graeber's 'The Utopia of Rules' this week — dense theorizing about bureaucracy, violence, and imagination made approachable in a bookstore's living room instead of a lecture hall. It's exactly the independent-bookstore-meets-radical-politics overlap that defines Iffy Books, one of the city's best venues for this. Free and drop-in friendly; come even if you skipped the first half, or just bring questions.
